title: Smooth Manifolds
purpose: Smooth manifolds from the definition to the de Rham theorem, opening with a targeted topology bridge: charts and atlases, smooth maps and the standard pathologies, the inverse and implicit function theorems, vector bundles and the tangent bundle, partitions of unity and embeddings, Sard's theorem, transversality and the Whitney theorems, the Lie derivative and Frobenius, differential forms and de Rham cohomology, studied from the MIT 18.965 (Fall 2004) lecture notes with Hitchin's Oxford notes as a second voice and original Corniversity exercises.
description:
A manifold is a space on which calculus makes sense: locally it looks like $\mathbb{R}^n$, and the local pictures are glued by smooth maps. This course builds that idea carefully and then uses it. It begins with a short, targeted bridge through the point-set topology the definition needs (Hausdorff, second countable, quotient topology), so that a learner who knows metric spaces but not general topology can start at once. It then treats smooth maps and the pathologies that justify the axioms, the derivative and the inverse and implicit function theorems, submanifolds and matrix groups, vector bundles and the tangent bundle, partitions of unity and the easiest Whitney embedding theorem, Sard's theorem, fibre bundles and the medium Whitney theorem, a Banach-space interlude on Fredholm operators and Smale's Sard theorem, transversality and the strong Whitney theorem, the Lie derivative and the Frobenius theorem, differential forms and de Rham cohomology, and finally Čech cohomology and the de Rham theorem.

**How this adaptation works.** The spine is the set of 26 per-lecture outline notes by Tomasz Mrowka for MIT OpenCourseWare 18.965 Geometry of Manifolds, Fall 2004 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), covering 35 sessions. Those notes are terse, so Corniversity lessons write out the definitions, proofs and examples in full, keep the notes' statement numbers (Definition 1.1, Theorem 5.1, …) so every citation can be reopened, and use Nigel Hitchin's author-hosted Oxford notes Differentiable Manifolds (2014; no licence stated, so reference-only) as a second presentation of charts, tangent vectors and forms. Corniversity re-paces the material as 12 units for a term of ten teaching weeks plus a reading week and a synthesis week, omits the Morse-theory lectures (the source provides no notes for them), and sets its own exercises with hint ladders and rubrics; no exercise is copied from the source problem sets.

**Prepared course.** All twelve units contain lecture notes, exact readings, original problems with progressive hints, instructor-only reference reasoning and cumulative synthesis. Some deep theorems have explicitly named source-proof dependencies or an identified proof-sketch boundary; these are stated in the relevant lessons. No course generation or subscription call is needed to study this authored material. Structural readiness does not imply external academic certification; review evidence and remaining limits are recorded separately.

outcomes.description: State the definition of a smooth manifold with all its topological hypotheses, verify it for the standard examples (spheres, projective spaces, Grassmannians, matrix groups) and explain by example why each hypothesis is needed.
outcomes.evidenceExpected: Accepted proofs that S^n and RP^n are smooth manifolds with explicit transition maps, and an accepted account of the line with two origins.

outcomes.description: Decide whether maps between manifolds are smooth, immersions, submersions or diffeomorphisms, using charts and the chain rule, and apply the inverse and implicit function theorems to produce submanifolds.
outcomes.evidenceExpected: Chart computations with chart-independence justified; a regular-value argument for a matrix group.

outcomes.description: Work with the tangent bundle and vector bundles: transition functions and the cocycle condition, pullbacks and Whitney sums, and the differential of a smooth map.
outcomes.evidenceExpected: Exercises identifying tangent spaces of submanifolds and verifying bundle constructions.

outcomes.description: Use partitions of unity and Sard's theorem to prove embedding and transversality results, stating exactly where second countability and compactness enter.
outcomes.evidenceExpected: A written proof of the easiest Whitney embedding theorem and a parametric-transversality argument with hypotheses named.

outcomes.description: Compute with differential forms and the exterior derivative, prove the Poincaré lemma, and explain de Rham cohomology and the Frobenius theorem.
outcomes.evidenceExpected: Unit11 calculation/cohomology sheets and exercise5 derive the homotopy operator identity and prove positive-degree Poincaré with the degree-zero qualification; unit10 exercise4 proves Frobenius in adapted coordinates.

outcomes.description: Explain the de Rham theorem: why Čech and de Rham cohomology agree, and what the acyclicity of the sheaf of forms contributes.

assessmentSpecs.title: Problem sets
assessmentSpecs.description: Each unit's exercises are submitted as immutable attempts and assessed with line-localised feedback. Revision is expected; the portfolio is the record of attempts and revisions, not a single mark.
rubricSummary: hypotheses and quantifiers (Hausdorff, second countable, compact, regular value)

assessmentSpecs.title: Mid-course synthesis: from charts to embeddings
assessmentSpecs.description: After unit 6: a written account of how the inverse function theorem, partitions of unity and Sard's theorem combine to embed a compact manifold in Euclidean space, with one worked example chosen by the learner. Open book, untimed by default.

assessmentSpecs.title: Final synthesis: the de Rham theorem
assessmentSpecs.description: An exposition of the de Rham theorem (Čech cohomology equals de Rham cohomology) with the Poincaré lemma and the acyclicity of the sheaf of forms proved or cited precisely, illustrated on a surface. Optional oral explanation to the tutor.

provenance.authoringMethod: Original course authoring completed directly in this Codex task with no runtime model/API generation. Primary MIT lecture PDFs were reopened and inspected on 2026-11-12; the source-map records verified URLs, file hashes, exact locator IDs and inspection limits. Existing useful early lessons were preserved and audited; new units include original proof explanations, problem sheets, hints, weighted rubrics and instructor reference reasoning.
reviewerNotes: The source's textbooks (Bott–Tu, Abraham–Marsden–Ratiu, Hirsch) are commercial and are not required; no acquisition request is needed for this course.
Lectures 23–28 (Morse theory) have no source notes and are omitted; lecture 35 (Smale's immersion theorem) is mentioned in unit 12 as further reading only.
Hitchin's notes carry no licence statement and are cited as reference-only; the course does not depend on importing them.
All twelve promised units are authored; independent source, solution and final review results live in the quality-loop evidence and must not be confused with author self-review.
Workload and teaching effectiveness have not been empirically validated with learners.

The strong Whitney theorem and global Reeb stability retain their advanced scope with explicit proof-sketch/imported-result boundaries; the course does not claim to supply a complete all-dimensions Whitney-surgery proof.
Unit11 exercise5 explicitly assesses the full homotopy/Poincaré proof; its independent post-repair check is tracked separately from author review.

Final independent academic review completed 2026-11-12: MATHS_REVIEW.md, with source-specific scope and limitations. Every current exercise has independently checked reference reasoning. Not human certification or measured learning effectiveness.

externalSyllabusNote: Adapted study path using MIT OpenCourseWare 18.965 Geometry of Manifolds (Fall 2004) lecture notes under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, with Nigel Hitchin's Differentiable Manifolds notes (Oxford, 2014) as a reference-only supplement. The original MIT course ran 35 sessions of 1.5 hours, was graded entirely on six problem sets, and assumed Analysis II and Algebraic Topology. Corniversity re-paces it as 12 units with an in-course topology bridge, omits the Morse-theory lectures, and sets its own exercises and assessments. This is not an MIT or Oxford course and confers no credit anywhere.
